title: Amazon MGM Studios Hires HBO Max’s Pia Barlow as Head of Original Series Marketing
description:

body:
HBO Max vet Pia Barlow has been hired as Amazon MGM Studios‘ new head of original series marketing.

	In her new role, which Barlow will begin Aug. 3, the exec will oversee all marketing efforts for Prime Video’s U.S. and Global Original Series. 

	Barlow will report directly to Sue Kroll, Amazon MGM Studios’ global head of marketing for film, series and brand. Barlow’s newly created position mirrors that of the studio’s VP of film marketing Stephen Bruno, who also reports to Kroll.
	

	“Pia brings an incredible amount of expertise and experience, gleaned over a number of years spent in every possible genre of film and television – and I can’t wait for her to meet and begin collaborating with all of you,” Kroll said in a memo to employees announcing Barlow’s hire Friday.


	Most recently, Barlow served as head of originals marketing for HBO Max, where she led campaigns for “The Pitt,” “Euphoria,” “House of the Dragon,” “Hacks” and HBO’s upcoming “Harry Potter” TV adaptation, among other projects.

	Prior to her time in that role at HBO Max, Barlow worked at Netflix on marketing for series including “Orange Is the New Black,” “Master of None,” “Making a Murderer” and “Queer Eye,” as well as growing the streamer’s international originals marketing strategy. 

	Barlow began her career at HBO in 2003 on marketing campaigns for “Girls,” “Boardwalk Empire,” and “Silicon Valley.” Since then, her additional roles have included SVP of marketing for Twentieth Century Fox Film, and an exec overseeing Netflix’s global creative and social media marketing campaigns for nonfiction and kids & family originals.

title: Spain’s World Cup Triumph Gets Prime Video Series
description: Prime Video is set to exclusively premiere worldwide a new docuseries about the Spanish National Team’s triumph at this year’s controversial and pol
body:
Prime Video is set to exclusively premiere worldwide a new docuseries about the Spanish National Team’s triumph at this year’s controversial and politically tainted FIFA World Cup — the feat that gave Spain its second World Cup winner’s star after trouncing Argentina in New Jersey.

	Produced by the Real Federación Española de Fútbol (RFEF) and Telefónica Broadcast Services (TBS), the as of yet untitled docuseries promises to offer exclusive behind-the-scenes access to the Spanish team and the lead up Ferran Torres’ extra time goal that secured Spain its 1-0 victory.  
	

	Featuring never-before-seen footage and testimonies from all the protagonists, viewers will have access to unique moments that examine the triumph of a group of 26 players and a coaching staff that, over 52 days, formed a family.


	More than just the thrill of victory, the docuseries examines the camaraderie and team effort, laughter and moments of tension and the looming challenge during a campaign when many even in Spain saw France as the favorite. Spain went on to beat France in the World Cup semi-final with a stunning exhibition of control soccer. 

	The show also promises “spectacle, entertainment and closeness to understand the keys to a success built on competitive instinct and the relentless drive to improve a team that will be remembered for the what, and, above all, for the how.”

	The docuseries, which will be available to Prime Video subscribers, marks the seventh collaboration between the RFEF and Prime Video, which is consolidating its position as the home of Spanish National Team content with a growing library of docuseries that offer worldwide fans exclusive access to the most intimate moments of each championship.
	

	Prime Video’s La Roja catalogue includes “Luis, el sabio del éxito,” about Spain’s 2008 UEFA Euro victory, and its architect, manager Luis Aragonés; “La Quinta de la quinta,” which follows young players aiming for a fifth Under-21 Euro title, the title echoing the description of Emilio Butragueño generation of  players in the 1980s ; and “La fuerza del grupo,” the inside story of the team’s 2020 UEFA European Football Championship shot; as well as “10 años de la primera estrella”; “La Copa de todos”; and “Un equipo llamado España.”

	In addition to films, series, documentaries and its own Amazon MGM Studios-produced movies and shows, sports is making up a major part of Prime Video programming. The streaming giant offers subscribers exclusive coverage of such live sport events as UEFA Champions League matches and NBA games in addition to acclaimed sports documentaries, among them “Built in Birmingham: Brady & the Blues,” “Sven” and the Amazon Original “All or Nothing” franchise, including “All or Nothing: Arsenal.”

title: ‘Emilia Pérez’ Director Jacques Audiard Reunites With Netflix for Horror Film (EXCLUSIVE)
description: After “Emilia Pérez” scored a best picture nomination at last year’s Oscars, Netflix is reuniting with French director Jacques Audiard on his next p
body:
After “Emilia Pérez” scored a best picture nomination at last year’s Oscars, Netflix is reuniting with French director Jacques Audiard on his next project, which will be an elevated horror film.

	Netflix has optioned “La Nuit ravagée” — a critically acclaimed horror novel by Jean-Baptiste Del Amo — and has tapped Audiard to develop a film adaptation, which will be a French-language Netflix original. Netflix had no comment.


	“La Nuit ravagée” is set in Saint-Auch, a fictional suburb on the outskirts of Toulouse in Southern France, in the early 1990s. It follows a group of teenagers drawn to an abandoned house that exerts a strange power on them. After one of their friends dies under disturbing circumstances, they decide to enter the house, not suspecting it’s alive with something supernatural. Once they enter it, it begins to feed on their private fears, desires and traumas, turning their psychological vulnerabilities into something monstrous and inescapable.
	

	Published by Gallimard last year, the book has been hailed as a loving homage to 1980s-90s horror films, especially Stephen King. It’s also been praised for skillfully blending fantasy and horror with social realism, confronting issues such as racism, homophobia and domestic violence, as well as capturing adolescent anxiety.

	Del Amo is best known for his 2016 novel “Le Règne Animal,” which was adapted into a French sci-fi adventure film directed by Thomas Cailley. The film world premiered at the Cannes Film Festival and won five Cesar Awards.

	The project will mark a departure for Audiard, who has never ventured into horror before. However, he is a strong match for the material because he’s built his career on stories about outsiders navigating brutal worlds in films like “A Prophet,” “Dheepan,” “Rust and Bone” and “Emilia Pérez.” He’s also expected to deliver more than a straightforward genre film, emphasizing the social realism aspects and sensory prose of the novel.
	

	Audiard is also known for always being up for a new challenge. His last directorial effort, “Emilia Pérez,” was a Spanish-language musical crime drama shot entirely in France, with a cast led by Karla Sofía Gascón, Zoe Saldaña, Selena Gomez and Adriana Paz. It won the jury prize at Cannes and made history with its best actress award given collectively to its four female leads. The film went on to earn 13 nominations at the Oscars and was considered a frontrunner for best picture. But in the lead-up to the ceremony, the movie campaign was rocked by a scandal involved offensive tweets by Gascón that had resurfaced. Still, “Emilia Pérez” won two Oscars: best supporting actress for Saldaña and original song. The movie also thrived at the Cesar Awards, winning seven awards out of 12 nominations, including best film.

	It’s also worth noting that horror is riding major commercial momentum right now on the heels of the year’s biggest breakout hits, “Backrooms” and “Obsession,” which grossed $387 million and $443 million worldwide, respectively.

	Since the project will be a Netflix original, it will likely skip a theatrical release in France, where windowing rules restrict the streamer’s access to theatrical movies for 15 months. Audiard is the latest high-profile international auteur working with Netflix on original films, following Guillermo del Toro, Lee Chang-dong and Fernando Meirelles, among others.

title: Costa Rican Below-the-Line Talents to Track
description: It’s been a long time coming but Costa Rica can now claim an Oscar-nominated below-the-line talent, sound and music editor Felipe Pacheco, who was r
body:
It’s been a long time coming but Costa Rica can now claim an Oscar-nominated below-the-line talent, sound and music editor Felipe Pacheco, who was recognized for his sound editing work on Ryan Coogler’s multi-Oscar winning “Sinners.”

	Based in Los Angeles, he moved there after earning a degree in film scoring at the prestigious Berklee College of Music. His extraordinary credits include Christopher Nolan’s epic Imax 70mm blockbuster “The Odyssey” and Oscar-winning “Oppenheimer,” “Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu” and Coogler’s “Black Panther: Wakanda Forever.” In television, he worked on Ben Stiller’s “Severance,” which snagged him an Emmy nomination.
	

	Throughout many of them, he has worked closely with Academy Award-winning composer Ludwig Göransson whom he first joined when they needed a Spanish-speaking music editor for the many Spanish songs in “Black Panther: Wakanda Forever.” His trial by fire came when Göransson asked him to join him on “Oppenheimer.” “We finished ‘Black Panther’ on a Friday, and that weekend Ludwig called: ‘I need you on ‘Oppenheimer’ Monday.’ I expected to join a team of music editors, but instead I was suddenly working alongside Nolan, learning his process on the fly. It was intimidating, especially as a young Costa Rican, but not knowing what I didn’t know may have worked in my favor. It all came together— and that’s why I was invited back for his next film.”


	That next film was “The Odyssey” where he relates that Nolan wanted to avoid the traditional orchestral sound often associated with historical epics. Instead, he asked Göransson to blend ancient Greek instruments with modern elements like synthesizers, creating a score that reflected a contemporary retelling of an ancient story. For the music team, it was a major creative challenge. Without the emotional power of strings or brass, they had to reinvent how the music conveyed intimacy and scale – using flutes, percussion and constant experimentation. “It was an absolute nightmare… but it was shockingly successful.”
	

	“Working on ‘Sinners’ was fun because it had a lot of on-set performances so they brought me in even from pre-production. The whole music team was working with the actors teaching them how to play instruments, how to sing and teaching them all the songs,” he recalls, adding that it was a highly collaborative job, with a lot of overlap between the music, dialogue and sound mixing departments.

	He worked closely with the production sound team to capture every performance on set, avoiding re-records. “We just didn’t want it to feel like a music video.”

	Here are five other Costa Rican Below-The-Line Talents to Track whose hard work and commitment to their craft may just earn them the ultimate reward in the future.

	José “Chisco” Arce, Colorist

	Through his production company, Maicero Prods, Arce has served as a colorist on a wide range of feature films, documentaries, episodic series and commercials. He has also worked as a filmmaker and cinematographer. His freelancer status has given him the freedom to tajke on jobs as far afield as Estonia, Saudi Arabia and Japan.

	His main task is to balance the images so they all have a consistent exposure and correct any issues that may have occurred during filming, he explains. “Then I create the film’s final look. For example, a horror film might have a darker, more desaturated palette, while a comedy would have a brighter, more vibrant feel.”

	His long list of credits takes in the Saudi Arabian fiction series “Kahilan,” Netflix Kuwait’s series, “The Exchange,” Japanese short “Together Alone” and Estonian short “Aurora Laul.”

	However, one of his most satisfying jobs has been closer to home, the Honduran film “Eva” by William Reyes.  “Although I joined the project later in the process, I collaborated closely with the director and cinematographer to shape the film’s visual progression. We designed a clear emotional arc: a warm, natural beginning, a darker and grayer middle as the story unfolds, and a final act that returns to a more hopeful reality. It worked very well for the film, which has been well received,” he says.

	Arce is currently working on a Colombian production that hasn’t been officially announced yet, but will be revealed next week as part of the Toronto International Film Festival lineup.
	

	Mauricio Esquivel, Production Designer

	Esquivel would really like to act, but in the meantime, he has become a much sought-after production designer, art producer and editor whose credits include some of the most acclaimed films to come out of Costa Rica and the region, including Cannes Director’s Fortnight title “Clara Sola,” Locarno multi-winner “I Have Electric Dreams,” Berlin Panorama Audience Awardee “Memories of a Burning Body” and most recently Neto Villalobos’ “Love is the Monster.”

	He has a degree in directing from the Veritas University and has written and directed two shorts, “Refugio” and “Pasajera.”

	“Each project has been challenging in a different way. ‘I Have Electric Dreams’ was my first time leading the art department on a feature film, so stepping into that role was a major challenge. But ‘Love is the Monster” was probably the most demanding because we were filming six hours away from San José, in a difficult production environment, with only four weeks to shoot. The film also had a complex dystopian, alternate-world aesthetic that required a lot of conceptual work.”

	Meanwhile, he is actively pursuing acting, currently training in the Meisner technique. “At heart, acting and directing are what I enjoy most, but I see every role as part of the same creative process. Sometimes a production design choice can achieve what a close-up or a line of dialogue cannot. If you want the audience to feel that a character is in love, for example, changing a costume from white to red might tell the story more effectively. That’s how I tend to think when conceptualizing a film, regardless of the role I’m in.”

	Nayuribe Montero, Sound Designer

	Based in Mexico, Montero has worked as a sound designer and production sound mixer over the past 10 years. She studied Film Sound at Cuba’s prominent International Film and Television School and holds a Master’s degree in Communication from the University of Costa Rica. Her credits include Edgar Ramirez-produced “It Would Be Night in Caracas” (Venice and TIFF), “Aurora”(Rotterdam) and “The Moon Will Contain Us” (Locarno).

	Of the recent pics she’s worked on, “It Would Be Night in Caracas” was probably the most arduous, she says. “The film was set in Venezuela, but we were shooting in Mexico, which created a lot of challenges. Many extras couldn’t use their own voices because their accents didn’t match, so we had to rebuild much of the sound in post-production with dubbing and additional recordings to create an authentic Venezuelan atmosphere. We also captured and collected many environmental sounds to help complete the world. It was a process of constant reconstruction and creativity, both in production and post, especially with so many extras and large crowd scenes.”
	

	Being a dancer has greatly informed her interest in filmmaking. “At film school, I started creating video dance pieces and became interested in documentary, so I’ve been exploring the intersection of both. Right now, I’m working on a documentary video dance project that combines these two worlds. For now, I feel more drawn to short films, although I’m not sure I’m ready to take on a feature yet,” she says.

	“I also learned that movement is not just about choreography. A professor, Silvina Szperling, an Argentine biodanza teacher, helped me understand movement as a form of expression and how the body communicates on its own. That’s what I focus on now—not simply filming a dance, but exploring the physical language and expressiveness of the body.”

	Kim Picado, Casting Director

	Picado has expanded her roles from casting director to acting coach and most recently, intimacy coordinator during her 15+ years in the biz. Her approach is also informed by her training in non-violent communication.

	She has worked as the casting director and acting coach on some of the top films from Costa Rica and elsewhere, including “Forever Your Maternal Animal” (Cannes 2026, Un Certain Regard), “I Have Electric Dreams” (Locarno 2022) and “If We Don’t Burn, How Do We Light Up the Night” (San Sebastian).

	She led the casting for the acclaimed “Clara Sola,” which earned her the Dams Award for Best Casting Direction at the Torino Film Festival.

	Reflecting on how she developed her career, she says: “When I started working in commercial casting, I noticed there was a gap between the language of audiovisual performance and the way actors were trained. Once I understood both worlds, I began creating processes that connected them. It became a personal mission, especially at a time when many directors preferred working only with non-professional actors.”

	“I created a role for myself within the filmmaking process: accompanying actors and directors from the very beginning of casting, through rehearsals and into the set. I support the direction and the performers throughout the process, especially during complex scenes. It’s almost like an assistant director role, focused entirely on acting,” she adds.

	Working on “I Have Electric Dreams,” which entailed working with children and a mix of professional and novice actors taught her that every film and every performer requires a unique approach. “Each process has to be designed individually, with a lot of attention to the actor’s needs and communication—something closely connected to my work in Nonviolent Communication.”
	

	She is currently working on “Quemada” by Ardelia Maurel and at an acting workshop in Ecuador led by director Sarahí Echeverría.

	Esteban Quesada, Line Producer

	Throughout his 17-plus years in the industry, Quesada has worked in Europe, Latin America, the U.S. and South Africa. His credits range from E! Entertainment TV’s “Keeping Up with the Kardashians” to the first “Paddington Bear” in the beloved franchise.

	He also made more than 10 documentaries on a variety of subjects, winning the best documentary award at the Chelsea Film Festival, New York with the docu “Joaquim Batica.”

	Quesada’s most recent line producing gig was with “Breaking Bad” creator-producer Mark Johnson on “Hope,” the debut fiction feature of Emmy-winning documentarian Abigail Fuller, “Hope.”

	“It was the first time Mark Johnson had worked in Costa Rica. He told me he’d been interested in filming there for years but the right project had never come along. The shoot lasted eight weeks, beginning with four weeks in the remote town of Pacaya, Cartago, followed by San José, where we filmed inside the National Theatre with support from the Costa Rican government. We also shot at several beaches and a waterfall in Guanacaste, showcasing a wide range of locations across the country.”

	Most importantly, several key creative roles were led by Costa Rican professionals, including costume and makeup. “That gave the local team a much greater creative voice and allowed the production to reflect Costa Rican culture more authentically.” The crew grew to around 150–200 people, bringing together professionals from Costa Rica, the United States and Mexico.

	For a line producer, budgeting is a key part of the process, he notes. “You have to calculate what the production will cost in the country, account for exchange rate fluctuations between the U.S. dollar and the Costa Rican colón, and factor in any available incentives.” For this project, they applied for Costa Rica’s 11.7% tax incentive, so all of those financial details had to be carefully considered throughout the planning process.

title: Film Commissions Step Up Role to Accelerate Growth In Central America and the Caribbean
description: The Ibero-American Film Commission Network, a non-profit organization that brings together film commissions and film offices across Ibero-America, t
body:
The Ibero-American Film Commission Network, a non-profit organization that brings together film commissions and film offices across Ibero-America, took place in the Costa Rica Media Market for the first time this year as it reaffirms its strategic commitment to developing the audiovisual ecosystem in Central America and the Caribbean. 

	IBEROFIC founder and president Carolina Cordero was present at the burgeoning industry event, which took place in San José on July 14-15, and held a series of meetings with producers, institutional representatives and key players in the regional industry. Organized by Costa Rica’s Film Commission, its Trade and Investment Promotion Agency (Promocomer), and tourism agency Essential Costa Rica, CRMM aims to bolster its position as a key platform for regional projects in the international market. The event is led by Costa Rica Film Commissioner Marysela Zamora. 
	

	Other participants at the Costa Rica Media Market included Senior Vice President of Acquisitions and Business Development at Utopia Distribution, Charlie Sextro; Manager of Physical Production at The Walt Disney Studios Michael Woolston; Cimarrón Cine’s Executive Director, Sandino Saravia; and Ari Cheren, from MrBeast’s Beast Industries. 


	“One of the most exciting developments this year is the mix of industry perspectives coming together,” Zamora told Variety ahead of the event kickoff. “We’re welcoming Disney, MrBeast, a new generation of producers working in Hollywood and leading players from countries like Mexico and Colombia — two of the region’s strongest audiovisual industries. Bringing them into conversation with talent from Central America and the Caribbean creates a unique space for new ideas, partnerships and a more connected regional industry.”
	

	During the market, Cordero met with Zamora, who is also a member of IBEROFIC’s board of directors, to develop initiatives aimed at promoting co-productions, attracting investment, creating specialized jobs, and strengthening regional capabilities through training programs, project advisory services, scholarships, and working groups.

	Participation in the Costa Rica Media Market is part of IBEROFIC’s expansion strategy, which seeks to strengthen regional cooperation, drive new co-productions, and consolidate the development of film commissions.

	Speaking about IBEROFIC’s commitment to fostering the industry in Central America and the Caribbean, Cordero said the region “possesses all the ingredients to become one of the most attractive territories for international audiovisual production: extraordinary location diversity, creative talent, increasingly professionalized industries and a clear willingness to work collaboratively.”

	“At IBEROFIC, we believe that audiovisual development depends not only on incentives but also on cooperation between countries, the strengthening of film commissions, and the creation of a regional strategy that enables global competitiveness,” concluded Cordero.

	With over 150 members across Ibero-America, IBEROFIC continues to establish itself as the leading regional facilitator connecting territories, producers, and institutions, thereby promoting a more integrated, competitive, and sustainable audiovisual industry. 

	Cordero’s visit to Costa Rica feeds into a wider picture in Latin America, as more countries inaugurate tax breaks and incentives. Mexico announced up to 30% of qualifying local production and post-production expenditures against income tax (ISR) on Feb. 15, joining countries such as Costa Rica itself in amping its financial efforts to attract international productions and bolster the local industry.

	In this scenario, the region has seen a steep increase in co-productions, especially between Latin American countries. 

	At this year’s CRMM, several Costa Rican co-productions with Panama and Guatemala were unveiled, with producers voicing their desire to continue to collaborate within Central America as well as strengthening their relationship with southern neighbors such as Colombia, Brazil and Argentina. 
	

	This movement emphasizes the need for solidified, well-structured film commissions to support projects navigating novel partnerships a national, regional and local levels. With European countries equally ramping up their offers and burgeoning markets such as Saudi Arabia and Jordan attracting major shoots, Latin American film commissions and audiovisual bodies have been bonding tighter together to make the continental and cultural region more enticing to ever-elusive large-scale productions.

schema.headline: Film Commissions Step Up Role to Accelerate Growth In Central America and the Caribbean

title: ‘The Dink’ Writer Sean Clements on His Funny, Heartfelt Tribute to the Pickleball Community: ‘I Got Adopted by This Whole Crew of Older Women’
description: Pickleball has exploded in popularity in the last decade as a variation of tennis that’s easier on bodies and simpler to pick up for people who want
body:
Pickleball has exploded in popularity in the last decade as a variation of tennis that’s easier on bodies and simpler to pick up for people who want to try something new. When comedy writer Sean Clements heard about a local turf war involving the low-impact sport, his brain started clicking.

	“A friend of mine who was involved in the L.A. Tennis Center was trying to get them to add more pickleball courts,” he says. “They only had one, and he wanted to expand, and was talking about all of these contentious meetings and how passionate — and sort of psychotic — everyone was on both sides of it. And I thought like, ‘OK, well, here’s a good backdrop and central conflict.’”
	

	The result is “The Dink,” a new Apple TV+ original movie debuting Friday on the platform. It stars “New Girl” alum Jake Johnson as a past-his-prime tennis pro Dusty Boyd who is encouraged to take up pickleball after he suffers an injury. Though he scoffs at the sport, he soon discovers a community that embraces him, including a friendly woman (Mary Steenburgen) who takes him under her wing. Along the way, his father (Ed Harris) tries to keep pickleballers from further encroaching on his tennis club.


	That storyline hit close to home for Clements, a high school tennis player who was having difficulties when he revisited the sport in his 30s. A few friends suggested pickleball could be gentler on his body, and he resisted, but when a writer friend brought him to play with a big group, he was all in.



	

					Writer and executive producer Sean Clements, director and executive producer Josh Greenbaum, and producers and actors Ben Stiller and Jake Johnson on the set of “The Dink.”
									Courtesy of Apple TV
	



	“I loved it,” he says. “I got hooked. So that became, ‘I’m this former tennis guy who got into the pickleball world,’ and there was a lot of animosity between those two camps. I started going to these open mixers and playing with total strangers, a lot of whom were retirement age. I found that I got adopted by this whole crew of older women who wanted to be partnered with me because I was a little more willing to run down the shots that were far away. That grew into them asking me if I wanted to meet up to play before the mixer, or if I wanted to go get bagels and coffee, or if we should all put together a dinner. The combination of this community embracing someone who is middle-aged, but being treated like they are a young superathlete, was a really good feeling and the kind of ego boost I always crave. That felt like there was a funny dynamic to play with there.”
	

	“The Dink” is a four-quadrant, PG-13 comedy that feels like a throwback to the Frat Pack aughts (there’s even a Ben Stiller cameo), but it’s a bit of a different gear for Clements, a prolific TV writer. His credits include cult hits like “Workaholics,” “Ash vs Evil Dead” and “Severance.” He also co-hosts the showbiz satire podcast “Hollywood Handbook,” which brings on big stars to clown on their persona and the inner workings of the entertainment industry, which incorporates plenty of dry, complex humor alongside his co-host, Hayes Davenport.

	How was Clements able to tailor his writing for a wide audience but still give them plenty of laughs? It first comes through the redrafting process.

	“The very initial draft and concept of this was a little closer to an ‘Eastbound and Down’-type voice for the character, where he was a little more caustic and aggressive,” Clements says. “As you work on it and you work with your collaborators and have table reads, you find what is working and resonating. We got to a point where when we were going to film, it actually had more curses in it. And we said, ‘That’s the only thing keeping this from being a PG-13,’ because there was no crazy violence or sex or anything. It occurred to us that, ‘If it’s just a little language adjustment to make this something that more people could like, then that’s pretty easy and something we should do.’”

	Clements also wanted to bring some warmth to the movie, echoing how he felt when he found his own pickleball community.

	“Maybe people who do listen to the podcast or know other stuff that I’ve done would be surprised by how much heart is in the movie,” he says. “A lot of that came from [director] Josh Greenbaum, who really encouraged me to find the emotion of these characters. But I also love that stuff. I’m a little bit of a softie. I think having the turns that put the characters into the situations where they can do the things that we want to see them do but still be surprising was a real goal.”

	Those comedic surprises were essential for Clements. As a big fan of sports movies — his favorites range from “Happy Gilmore” and “Major League” to “Without Limits” and “Moneyball” — he knew there were certain moments that fans would expect, but some of the biggest laughs would come from giving them a tweak or subversion.
	

	“In any movie like this, there are certain beats that you are going to crave from it,” he says. “You don’t want to shortchange the audience from some of those moments: Seeing the person get better at the thing, or seeing how they are unable to gut it out against the opponent they’re overmatched by. There are beats that I want in these movies. Some of them are classic, but can you make them not feel cliché by finding a more interesting path to get to them?”

	Clements is currently hard at work filming a pilot for Hulu called “Lex,” but would he ever be interested in another story set in the “Dink”-iverse? A chance encounter provided an interesting idea.

	“On one of the other interviews we did, one of the guys said that pickleball courts were taking over the basketball courts at the gym that he was a member of,” Clements says. “And I thought, ‘Well, I hadn’t had an idea for a sequel, but man, that’s real potential. They’re at war with the basketball players instead of the tennis players. That’s heightening.’”

	Watch the trailer for “The Dink” below.

schema.headline: ‘The Dink’ Writer Sean Clements on His Funny, Heartfelt Tribute to the Pickleball Community: ‘I Got Adopted by This Whole Crew of Older Women’

title: Andrés Madrigal Explores Costa Rica’s Little-Known Queer History Through Personal Doc ‘Lost Men’
description: When his grandfather passed away, director Andrés Madrigal felt an urge to pick up his camera and capture every possible moment of that immediate gr
body:
When his grandfather passed away, director Andrés Madrigal felt an urge to pick up his camera and capture every possible moment of that immediate grief. This archival impulse would eventually become Madrigal’s feature debut “Lost Men,” which has its world premiere at the Costa Rica Film Festival.

	The intimate doc chronicles Madrigal’s personal family history in the aftermath of the patriarch’s death. The elderly man, who died in a fire in 2019, was married for 57 years in conservative Costa Rica. Following his passing, the director’s father finally shares a long-kept secret: the Madrigal family head was a closeted gay man. Father and son then recollect a life lived in secret as the filmmaker reflects on his own queerness. 
	

	Speaking with Variety ahead of the film’s premiere, Madrigal says he first had an impulse to make the film as a way of not losing any more memories of his grandfather. “ A lot of his writings and memories were gone forever,” he adds. “It started with that archival and emotional interest to a personal or mostly a familiar extent. I gradually realized this story was shaping up to be something more and that it almost demanded to be told outside of my nuclear family.”


	Given his desire to bring long-kept family secrets to a very public light, the director and his father spent a long time discussing the logistics and the boundaries of making the film. “This story touches on many family wounds that were reopened after both my grandparents passed away,” he says. “Because of that, I decided to work at a production rhythm that allowed both my father and me not only to make the film, but also to process any feelings that might emerge through the telling of this story.”
	



	

					‘Lost Men’  Courtesy of Blue Paradox Films
	



	“I always referred to the interviews as conversations, and we established ground rules, such as stopping whenever either of us felt the need to,” he notes. “We also approached things gradually, moving from easier topics to more difficult ones. Thankfully, my dad and I already had a very close relationship before making the film, and I think that comes across on screen. We trusted each other deeply throughout the process, and I believe that trust was key to making the film possible.” 

	While “Lost Men” keeps a tight focus on Madrigal’s personal family history, the documentary also briefly delves into the Costa Rican queer scene, with glimpses of the country’s nightlife and the director’s friend circle. Madrigal wanted to explore themes of “queerness, masculinity and memory” through “the lens of my family first and foremost,” but felt it was important to portray his country’s queer culture because it felt “representative” of him as a character.

	“It was a very conscious decision to include footage of San José’s queer nightlife,” he says. “I also included elements of my private queer sphere, such as my friends and my ex-partner. Although these aspects are deeply personal, they also reflect broader dimensions of queer life in Costa Rica,” he goes on, noting that he believes in the maxim of “personal as political” — “In my grandfather’s case, for example, understanding the limitations and complexities of his life also speaks to a broader reality in Costa Rica at the time.”

	Asked about the challenges of realizing the film, Madrigal mentions the complexities of “understanding the delicate balance between telling a deeply personal family story with the care and sensitivity it required, while also separating myself enough to gain perspective and evaluate it as I would any other fiction or scripted project I was directing.”

	“At the same time, having to both direct the film and include myself as one more character within the story was definitely daunting at first,” he adds. “With the help of Luis Diego Pérez, the film’s editor, we managed to strike that balance between telling a very vulnerable story and remembering that we were ultimately telling it for a broader audience.”
	

	As for the joys of the process, the director recalls the thrills of rediscovering his grandfather’s literary work, as well as tightening his relationship with his family, and forming a close bond with the crew. “There was a great deal of trust between us, and joy and spontaneity were always part of the process. That sense of play became an essential part of how the film was made. I think a lot of the credit for that goes to Sofia Meza Herrera, the film’s producer, who consistently protected and nurtured that atmosphere of safety and care throughout the process.”



	

					‘Los Men’.  Courtesy of Blue Paradox Films
	



	Commenting on making “Lost Men” as a Costa Rica-Guatemala co-production, Blue Paradox Films producer Sofía Meza Herrera notes how “lucky” she is to be part of a generation of Central American producers “surrounded by new industry opportunities and great mentors who understand both the challenges of filmmaking and the amazing artistic drive within the isthmus.” 

	“Our industry has been connecting with each other through film festivals and workshops, networking talents from different generations and having international mentors who put in the effort of understanding the Central American panorama to further strengthen our talent,” she adds. “I’ve grown to believe in Central-American Cinema as an alliance without borders. Creating film in this region is inherently political, and sharing our resources to further our opportunities, talent and audiences is as well.”

	“In Central America, there are a lot of stories to be told, but few resources to take them to the big screen,” says Felipon Díaz of Guatemala’s 4:4:4 Televisión. “When I encountered ‘Lost Men,’ I connected with Andrés and Sofía, their beautiful energy and the energy of the project, an intimate and personal story that I found necessary to be told in the current times that we are living.”

	“Lost Men” is produced by Madrigal and Meza Herrera’s Blue Paradox Films in co-production with Guatemala’s 4:4:4 Televisión, led by Felipon Díaz. The film was supported by Costa Rica’s El Fondo Fauno and the Netherlands’ Prince Claus Seed Award.

schema.headline: Andrés Madrigal Explores Costa Rica’s Little-Known Queer History Through Personal Doc ‘Lost Men’

title: Anne Hathaway’s Oscars ‘Odyssey’: Will She Campaign for Lead Actress or Supporting?
description:
“Ithaca’s king is coming home.” But when Oscar season arrives, where will the Academy welcome back its queen?

	Christopher Nolan‘s “The Odyssey” op
body:
“Ithaca’s king is coming home.” But when Oscar season arrives, where will the Academy welcome back its queen?

	Christopher Nolan‘s “The Odyssey” opened to a massive box office haul and an avalanche of critical praise, vaulting it to the front of the Oscar race months before the fall festivals begin. But the question already dominating awards conversations isn’t whether the film will contend (we already know it will). It’s where Universal will elect to campaign Oscar winner Anne Hathaway, who plays Penelope, wife of Odysseus (Matt Damon) and mother of Telemachus (Tom Holland), fending off suitors in her husband’s absence.
	

	Lead or supporting? It’s the season’s first real strategic inquiry among awards enthusiasts, and the Academy’s own record book argues both ways — including one cautionary precedent from Nolan’s last epic to which Hathaway’s team will have to pay very special attention.


	Universal is expected to mount an aggressive awards campaign, hoping to deliver Nolan a second best picture and best director victory just three years after “Oppenheimer.” In Variety’s Oscar analysis, our current projection shows a path that tops out at 17 nominations. Sixteen would tie the record set just last season by Ryan Coogler’s “Sinners,” which surpassed the long-standing mark of 14 shared by “All About Eve” (1950), “Titanic” (1997) and “La La Land” (2016).

	However, don’t expect an answer anytime soon. Nolan has long avoided awards strategy conversations until well after a film opens, meaning category discussions with the studio and talent are unlikely to begin in earnest until later this fall — at least not formally.
	

	For Hathaway, “The Odyssey” anchors a busy year that has already included the blockbuster “The Devil Wears Prada 2,” and the well-received (but financially disappointing) “Mother Mary.” Still to come are the end-of-summer thriller “The End of Oak Street” and the Colleen Hoover adaptation “Verity.”

	Vote splitting across multiple films is unlikely to be Hathaway’s biggest concern. The more pressing question is which category offers the clearest path to a nomination — and perhaps a second Oscar after “Les Misérables” (2012) in supporting actress. In addition, there’s also the matter of whether her placement will help or hurt another viable contending co-star: Samantha Morton, whose Circe has drawn some of the film’s loudest raves.

	The good news for Hathaway is that whatever is ultimately chosen, there isn’t a category fraud debate to be had. Every year we have a few contenders that can go either way, depending on how voters feel. Think back to examples like Maria Bello in “A History of Violence” (2005) or Meryl Streep in “The Devil Wears Prada” (2006). 

	There’s a compelling argument for either category, based on audience reaction and on the voters themselves. And interestingly, the Oscar history books read like a coin flip.



	

									Melinda Sue Gordon
	



	Let’s start with the basics. Across his entire filmography, Nolan’s films have produced only four acting nominations. The good news for whoever gets campaigned: three of those four converted. Heath Ledger won supporting actor for “The Dark Knight” (2008). Cillian Murphy won lead actor and Robert Downey Jr. won supporting actor for “Oppenheimer” (2023). So while Nolan’s performers rarely earn acting nominations, when they do, they often win.

	The bad news is that fourth name, and it belongs to one of Hathaway’s “besties.”

	The last time Nolan built a sprawling ensemble around a great man, making perilous choices and handing the wife the emotional load, that actress was Emily Blunt in “Oppenheimer.” She campaigned in supporting, was nominated, and eventually lost to Da’Vine Joy Randolph in “The Holdovers” — on a night when “Oppenheimer” won seven Academy Awards, including best picture, director and both of the other acting categories it was up for.

	That is a scenario Universal and Hathaway’s team have to game out. Like Blunt’s Kitty Oppenheimer, Penelope serves as the emotional anchor while her husband’s story unfolds elsewhere. It’s a role the Academy frequently nominates but one that doesn’t always translate into a win.
	

	Of the 90 supporting actress winners in Oscar history, 56 of them (or 62%) came from a film nominated for best picture. Still, only 14 (or 16%) came from the film that actually won it. Riding the year’s juggernaut gets you on the ballot, but it does not, often enough, get you to the podium.

	But if a studio wants to double dip in an acting category, supporting actress is where it works best — the race most likely to recognize two or more performers from the same film. It has happened 37 times, compared with 23 in supporting actor, 12 in lead actor and only five in lead actress. If Universal campaigns Hathaway in supporting alongside Morton, it’s the most common double-double in Academy history.

	The problem is how rarely one of those women walks away with the trophy. In those 37 cases, one of the two nominees won 13 times (or 35%). That means nearly two out of three times, a film lands two supporting actress nominations, and both women go home empty-handed. It happened as recently as last season, when “Sentimental Value” put up Elle Fanning and Inga Ibsdotter Lilleaas and the category went to Amy Madigan for “Weapons.”

	When you sort those 37 films by how they fared in best picture, it actually reveals an illuminating pattern. I grouped every case into three buckets and tracked how often one of the two nominated actresses actually won:


When the film won best picture: eight cases, six winners (or 75%).


“Gone with the Wind” (1939), “Mrs. Miniver” (1942), “Gentleman’s Agreement” (1947), “Kramer vs. Kramer” (1979), “Chicago” (2002) and “Everything Everywhere All at Once” (2022) all produced a supporting actress winner. Only “All About Eve” (1950) and “Tom Jones” (1963) went home empty-handed.



When the film was nominated for best picture but lost: There were 17 cases, and five winners (or 29%).


Helen Hayes for “Airport” (1970), Cloris Leachman for “The Last Picture Show” (1971), Jessica Lange for “Tootsie” (1982), Melissa Leo for “The Fighter” (2010) and Octavia Spencer for “The Help” (2011)



When the film missed best picture entirely: There are 12 cases and only two winners (or 17%). Tatum O’Neal for “Paper Moon” (1973) and Dianne Wiest for “Bullets Over Broadway” (1994).



	So in other words, the double is a strong play only if Universal genuinely believes “The Odyssey” is winning the top prize. Short of that, it has produced far more consolation nominations than statuettes.

	So what about a lead actress run? Well, no Nolan film has ever produced a lead actress nominee. Campaigning Hathaway in lead would ask Academy voters to recognize the first female lead performance of his career — and for a studio that has openly signaled it wants history alongside its trophies, that’s the kind of hook voters can repeat back to one another. That would open up the possibility of “The Odyssey” joining the list of 15 other films that have been nominated in all four acting categories, which began with “My Man Godfrey” (1936) to “American Hustle” (2013). 

	There’s a risk to this move. 

	Campaigning what some may perceive as a supporting role in lead can leave a performance just outside the lineup, as it did for Richard Gere in “Chicago” (2002) and Chase Infiniti in “One Battle After Another” (2025) — both best picture winners, and both had four other acting noms that missed out in a key category.
	



	

									Universal Pictures
	



	Obviously, Morton’s possible return could complicate matters further. Nolan shared publicly that her Circe drew an on-set ovation from the crew, something he hadn’t seen since Ledger on “The Dark Knight.” That’s a valuable endorsement for the season ahead. She’s also carrying her own narrative that supporting actress can reward. Morton has two previous noms, supporting for “Sweet and Lowdown” (1999) and lead for “In America” (2003), and hasn’t been on a ballot since. An overdue veteran with an unforgettable single sequence in a prestige juggernaut is, on paper, precisely what the Academy membership could find irresistible.

	If forced to project today, I’d lean toward supporting as the safer route to a nom, but whether it yields a win depends almost entirely on whether Morton’s buzz turns out to be real.

	Universal has until fall festival season to decide, and history offers compelling arguments for either strategy with no definitive answer. That’s precisely what makes Hathaway’s category placement one of the season’s earliest — and most fascinating — Oscar questions.

schema.headline: Anne Hathaway’s Oscars ‘Odyssey’: Will She Campaign for Lead Actress or Supporting?

title: ‘Her Private Hell’ Director Nicolas Winding Refn on Ignoring Critics, Why the Government Must Regulate AI and Planning His Third Film With Ryan Gosling
description: Nicolas Winding Refn‘s 11th film, “Her Private Hell,” is a long way away from the grounded work many fans are familiar with, like “Drive” and “Brons
body:
Nicolas Winding Refn‘s 11th film, “Her Private Hell,” is a long way away from the grounded work many fans are familiar with, like “Drive” and “Bronson.” The feature, now in theaters via Neon, is a neon-drenched sci-fi tale of an actress, Elle (Sophie Thatcher), a soldier, Private K (Charles Melton) and a killer known as Leatherman who move around a futuristic city in a dreamy fog. It’s a sexy, sweaty and divisive film, which premiered at Cannes to mixed reviews but is certain to draw a cult audience, like his most recent movie, 2016’s “The Neon Demon,” to which “Hell” feels like a mysterious and fashionable companion piece.
	

	The Danish filmmaker spoke to Variety about the ideas behind “Hell,” its bombastic score, creating the unique visuals and much more.

	
		Where did the idea for “Her Private Hell” come from? It’s much different from your other work.	

	In a way, you can say everything I’ve done has led to this film, because it’s a kind of an amalgam of everything that I’ve ever done, everything that I like to see. So that’s how it all began. But also freeing myself from conventions in a day and age of algorithms.
	
		There are so many striking images in the film. Are there some you pictured even before you developed the story and wrote the script [with cowriter Esti Giordani]?	

	It all started with two ideas. I had an idea of Private K going to hell. And then I had an idea of a young woman coming to a city that doesn’t exist. What combined them was that they were both very artificial, because they were set in worlds that didn’t exist. But in order to connect them together, they needed the tip of a triangle. That became Leatherman, because he would service both storylines.
	
	
		When developing ideas like “a city that doesn’t exist,” what were the conversations you had with your DP about the look and feel?	

	I said it had to have a lot of color, almost like color candy. Everything had to be very fluffy, so you’d want to eat it like whipped cream with injected color coats. It needed to be an opera, with everything that comes with that.
	
		Was there a moment when connecting with Sophie Thatcher that you knew she would be the perfect Elle?	

	We’d been casting for a year, and Sophie came in very late for a general meeting. Right when I saw her, I just knew it was her. She had a wonderful audition, but I’d already made up my mind that she was the one, purely on instinct. I don’t know what it was. There was something about her that intrigued me. She had these eyes that were incredibly seductive, like an old movie star. Because she had to carry the movie, once she was in play, everything started to fall into place. But it took a year or so.
	
		Since you’ve been working in TV, this is your first film since “The Neon Demon.” What made you want to pivot back to features?	

	I think that had more to do with a human desire to preserve cinemas. Cinemas have always been the cheapest form of entertainment that we collectively could experience together. It’s always been the lowest common denominator for all of us to meet on equal terms. In today’s world, so much digitalization is not necessarily healthy for the mind or the soul, for that matter. I want to make films for cinemas. I feel like, by law, every village in the world should have a single-screen cinema. We’re getting so divided by the politicians, so when they’ve stolen all our money and created all the wars, it is what brings us together. But it’s not so much what you see, it’s how you see it. We can all sit on our isolation pads and experience this, see something, which we all do. I do it, and I think it’s a beautiful invention. I wouldn’t want to not have that. But I think for the human soul, we also need to come together.
	
		Are you able to make it to the movie theater as much as you’d like to these days?	

	My youngest and I, we go to the movies.
	
		Have there been some recent films that have stuck with you?	

	I like to see everything. It’s a different world out there from when I was younger in terms of what’s getting made and so forth. But there are still a lot of good films, and it’s hard to kind of pinpoint anything specific because it’s not so much about the film. It’s the fact that I feel good about going to a movie theater of quality and handing them my hard-earned money, because I think that it’s a contribution. It’s like going into a video store that still operates, or a record store or a bookshop. You feel you are servicing a higher purpose.
	
	
		Making a film is hard work. What drives you to do it?	

	What drives me? I wear my emotions on my sleeve, and if I can’t find a way to release them, I’ll probably be unbearable to be around. So in a way, I’m making the world a better place by not being unbearable.
	
		Is there any therapeutic value that you feel once you’ve shot your film?	

	Filming the actual production is only half the work. So I always divide it up into four sections: thinking up the idea, writing the script, shooting the script and all the completion of post. Those four stages are four ways to change the entire project. Obviously, it gets more and more difficult from the practicalities, but still, you can completely change things. Then when it gets to the actual post-production, you’re dividing it up into three sections. There’s visuals, music and sound. So of the fourth section, there are actually three separate categories that still need to be aligned. It’s not until the film is completely done, meaning that’s when you deliver to the nest an egg, that’s when you let go.
	
		The legendary Pino Donaggio, who has worked on countless legendary genre films and is a key Brian De Palma collaborator, provides the showstopping score to this movie. What were your discussions with him about the music?	

	It was the only movie I made where I didn’t have a sound in my mind. I didn’t have a clear idea of the music, which I’d never really tried before. But I also think it was God saying to me, “You need to make that opera you’ve always wanted to make.” Once I accepted the terms from God, I had to find a composer who did film music and opera. Where else can you go but Italy? There I discovered all the composers were dead from that period that you and I would define as the golden era of soundtracks, film music and so forth. The only one that was alive was Pino Donaggio, who, in a way, was the best one because I’d used his past scores as reference or inspiration music. It seemed there’s a meaning here, there’s a path. 

	So I met with Pino, who was basically in semi-retirement, in his mid-80s. I asked him if he wanted to write an opera. He said, “Absolutely.” And I said, “But you’re going to die soon. Could you make it a requiem?” He found that very funny, so we had great humor. I also made it very clear that in an opera apparatus you start with the music — now, I’m actually ending with the music. So I’ve built this entire infrastructure with veins, and there’s a heart but there’s no blood. “Your music is going to be the blood that ties the entire movie together. So I’m betting my one chip, my one black chip on one number, and you’re the guy. Good luck.” The music … it was luck; it was fantastic to hear. 
	

	One of my favorite memories was sitting in Rome after we had done the mix and Pino had a little too much wine, and he started imitating Elvis Presley. I thought, “That’s fuckin’ cool.”
	
		Your work inspires so much conversation — do you engage with any of it? Do you read anything written about your art?	

	You don’t engage. It’s no longer your world. It’s everyone else’s, and you’re just an observer. I just go back to my gardening.
	
		What’s been the focus in your garden lately?	

	The problem is I don’t know how to garden. So I basically just play Legos instead. I build flowers out of Lego.
	
		That’s beautiful.	

	I just got the Tintin Rocket, which is just absolutely amazing, and I’m looking forward to building it. It’s a great way to be creative without making an effort, other than just putting blocks together of plastic.
	
		Have you been approached at all by people in the AI world? Is that something you have any interest in learning about?	

	I think AI is a difficult discussion because it’s always narrowed down to one thing: good or bad. I think we need to separate the silos a little bit. From a social academic effect, I’m obviously very concerned because I don’t think having fewer people with opportunities is a healthy way for society to exist. The inequality that’s already skyrocketing is by no means a positive evolution. I don’t like the people that represent that world very much, at least I haven’t met anyone yet. I’m not saying they’re not amazing visionaries, but a vision comes with a responsibility. 

	I’m a humanitarian. I believe in the goodness of humans. I believe that we find happiness in common sharing. I think AI is good for revolutionizing certain aspects of the medical industry or information, and certain access to information. At the same time, it’s messed with our already reconstructed reality. I’m concerned about it there very much. But as a creative tool, meaning just a brush, I’m very intrigued by it. But is it going to have consequences? Absolutely. Do I condemn those? Absolutely. Do I think it should be regulated? Absolutely. Does it need to be controlled by an outside body? Absolutely. I think it’s a government responsibility, the same way that the government offers water and the internet.
	
		It was recently the 15th anniversary of “Drive,” and fans have been revisiting your work with Ryan Gosling. You’re both very busy, but do you think there’ll be some collaboration again if the timing works out?	

	It’s the only thing we ever talk about. Besides all the other things that go through our minds, it always comes down to that essence of “When are we going to do it again?” We know we have a third movie in us. We just have to find the one. But once you know it, you’re halfway there.
	
	
		Your next movie is a “Maniac Cop” reimagining. What can fans expect from your new vision?	

	Oh, it’s like Christmas. You gotta wait until the tree comes, and the packages will arrive with Santa Claus.
	
		Was it always a favorite film of yours?	

	I like the concept. I bought the rights many years ago, and I’ve sat on it, and there have been numerous opportunities to try to make it, but maybe it was never the right time. I very much believe in faith and the right time. Now’s the right time, and it was also easy for me to put it together, and we are shooting next year in L.A.

	Watch the “Her Private Hell” trailer below.

schema.headline: ‘Her Private Hell’ Director Nicolas Winding Refn on Ignoring Critics, Why the Government Must Regulate AI and Planning His Third Film With Ryan Gosling

title: ‘Reacher’ Star Alan Ritchson Slams ‘F—ing Pedophiles’ in Politics: ‘I Would Get Those Epstein Files Out in Two Seconds … Bitch, Move’
description: “Reacher” star Alan Ritchson got fired up about politics on the latest episode of Josh Horowitz’s “Happy Sad Confused” podcast, spouting off about t
body:
“Reacher” star Alan Ritchson got fired up about politics on the latest episode of Josh Horowitz’s “Happy Sad Confused” podcast, spouting off about the Epstein files and the “fucking rapists” in politics.

	“The fucking Epstein files! God damn it! Where are they? It’s a fucking law, bitch. Show it, you fucking pedophiles,” Ritchson said. “I shouldn’t say ‘fuck’ because I’m a Christian, and people are gonna go, ‘How can he say fuck and he’s a Christian?’ Because that is something that should make you want to say ‘fuck.'”
	

	In classic Jack Reacher fashion, Ritchson continued: “This is my fucking politics, dude: I would fucking railroad these fuckers. I would get those Epstein files out in two seconds. Fucking move out of the way. Like, get out of there. I don’t care what room they’re in. Bitch, move. Give me the fucking manila envelope. I will get you the Epstein files. Don’t you want to see what’s in there so that we can hold people accountable? These fucking rapists! We’re just cool with it?” 


	Without naming names, the hulking action star seemed to turn his attention to a politician with quite a lot of power. “That bitch has the keys to the nuclear. He’s, like, all up into 13-year-olds. Like, dude, what? Go to jail. Go to jail.”

	Ritchson prefaced the rant by joking that his publicist is somewhere “biting her nails” and saying he is “missing” the gene that makes some actors “afraid to speak their mind.” “Everybody is scared around me for what I’m going to say,” Ritchson said, adding that he is not a “loose cannon,” he’s just “saying the shit that everybody should say if they give a shit about humanity.”
	

	Ritchson also talked about his friendship with fellow action star and former California Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, who he said “really wanted” Ritchson to get into politics. He hasn’t exactly ruled it out but said he isn’t yet ready to retire from acting.

	“There’s going to come a time where maybe I feel like I’m either well resourced enough or visible enough to really make an impact in many people’s lives,” Ritchson said. “I care deeply about the outliers, the maligned people who have very difficult lives, people who are forgotten and overlooked and unwanted and unloved. I care deeply about making the world more fair and free for those people.”

title: 'Roseanne' Star Sara Gilbert Sells L.A. Farmhouse for $8.5 Million
description:

                          Offloads L.A. Home For $8.5 Million
body:
'Roseanne' Sara Gilbert
                          Offloads L.A. Home For $8.5 Million
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              July 24, 2026
                            9:04 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
            Sara Gilbert's made a big bang on the real estate market this week ... because she just sold her Los Angeles home for more than $8 million.
      
    
            The sitcom actress closed the deal on her 6-bedroom, 7-bathroom L.A. farmhouse Wednesday ... parting with her home for $8.45 million.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The 6,388-square-foot home sits on 0.36 acres of land near historic Hancock Park in L.A.'s Mid-City neighborhood.
      

            The house overlooks a ritzy country club in the area and features skylit vaulted ceilings, a large outdoor deck, a pool and a spa ... certainly some amenities the Connors couldn't afford!
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Sara's been trying to sell this pad for more than a year now ... originally listing the place for around $11 million in April 2025.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            It appears Sara will make a tidy profit on the place despite bringing the price down a couple of times ... she bought it back in 2016 for $6,850,000.
      
    
            Jamie Sher of the Sher Group and Jonah Wilson of Carolwood Estates held the listing.

body:
Nolan Wells
                          Sister of Girl He Allegedly Stayed Behind With at Horn Island Speaks Out
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              July 24, 2026
                            9:28 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Nolan Wells' friends say he hung back on Horn Island with a girl when they left in their boat ... but the girl is apparently telling a different story.
      
    
            19-year-old Katie McCormack spent time with Nolan on the island before his disappearance and death, according to the Daily Mail ... and Nolan's friend, Warren Hudson, says their group was frantically rushing off the island as their vessel took on water ... claiming Nolan refused to leave Katie and join them on their journey back to the Mississippi mainland.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Thing is ... Katie's sister, Gracie, told the Daily Mail ... "Katie had a conversation and assumed that Nolan was getting ready to get on the boat he came out on."
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Katie's sister added ... "Katie assumed the 'friends' telling him to get on the boat wouldn't have left him."
      
    
            As you know, 18-year-old Nolan never made it home from Horn Island ... and his body was found July 6 in its shallow waters ... near where he was last seen alive.
      
    
            Investigators are still trying to piece together what led up to Nolan's death ... and his family commissioned an independent autopsy.
      
    
            Preliminary findings revealed he may have suffered a head injury ... but there's no official cause or manner of death yet.
